scenes.title:
Prompt Caching
[[Pay once, reuse many times]]
scenes.subtitle: Make Claude cheaper and faster when your prompt repeats

lines.say: Your help desk bot sends the same long handbook to Claude with every single question. And you pay for it every single time.
Prompt caching fixes that. In this video, you'll learn what it is, how it works, and when to use it.
Then we'll add it to a real Python app, step by step, and measure the savings.

scenes.heading: What is [[prompt caching]]?
items: Claude **stores the start** of your prompt, the **prefix**
Later requests with the same prefix **reuse it**

lines.say: So, what is prompt caching?
Claude reads your whole prompt on every request. With prompt caching, it stores the start of the prompt, called the prefix.
The next request that starts with exactly the same prefix reuses it, instead of processing it again.
Think of a teacher who already read the textbook. For the next question, they don't reread it from page one.
Reading from the cache costs much less, and Claude starts answering faster. The easiest way to turn it on is one field: cache control, type ephemeral.

scenes.heading: Write once, [[read many times]]

rows.label: The prefix
rows.text: tools → system → messages, **up to the breakpoint**

rows.label: First request
rows.text: **Writes** the cache: 1.25× the normal input price

scenes.banner: The cache lives 5 minutes, and every hit resets the timer

lines.say: Here's how it works.
Claude reads a request in a fixed order: tools, then the system prompt, then the messages. The prefix is everything up to a point you mark, called the cache breakpoint.
The first request writes the prefix to the cache. That costs a little more: one and a quarter times the normal input price.
Every request after that reads it, for a tenth of the price. On the newest models, like Claude Sonnet 5.5, it's even a twentieth.
lines.tts: Every request after that reads it, for a tenth of the price. On the newest models, like Claude Sonnet five point five, it's even a twentieth.

lines.say: The cache lives five minutes by default, and every time it's used, the timer starts again, for free.

left.title: Use it when…
left.body:
• The start of your prompt
  stays the same
• Long instructions, a handbook,
  documents, tool definitions
• Long chats and agents
• Many requests in a row

right.title: Skip it when…
right.body:
• The prompt is short
  (under 512 tokens on the
  newest models: not cached)
• The start changes every time
• One-off requests, far apart

lines.say: When should you use it?
When the start of your prompt stays the same across many requests: long instructions, a handbook, documents, tool definitions, long chats and agents.

Skip it for short prompts. Under the minimum, 512 tokens on the newest models, nothing is cached at all. And skip it when the start of the prompt changes every time, or for one-off requests far apart.
lines.tts: Skip it for short prompts. Under the minimum, five hundred and twelve tokens on the newest models, nothing is cached at all. And skip it when the start of the prompt changes every time, or for one-off requests far apart.

lines.say: Our use case: a help desk bot for Maple Mugs, the small online shop from my earlier videos. It answers customers using the store's handbook.
Without caching, every question sends the whole handbook, about 1,500 tokens, at full price.
lines.tts: Without caching, every question sends the whole handbook, about fifteen hundred tokens, at full price.

lines.say: With caching, the handbook is written once. Then every question reads it, for a twentieth of the price.
Here's the handbook: products, shipping, returns, care. About a thousand words.

do.text:
# Maple Mugs customer handbook

Maple Mugs is a small online shop that sells handmade ceramic mugs, bowls and teapots. Everything is made by four potters in our studio in Vermont. This handbook is the only source of truth for answering customers. If the answer is not in this handbook, say so and offer to pass the question to the team at help@maplemugs.example.

## How to talk to customers

- Be warm, short and clear. Two to four sentences is usually enough.
- Use the customer's words. If they say "cup", don't correct them to "mug".
- Never promise a date, a refund or an exception that this handbook does not allow.
- If a customer is upset, apologize once, then focus on what we can do.
- Always end with one clear next step for the customer.

## Our products

- **Classic Mug** (12 oz): our best seller. Six glazes: Maple, Moss, Slate, Cream, Ocean and Ember.
- **Big Morning Mug** (16 oz): the Classic Mug, but taller. Same six glazes.
- **Espresso Cup** (3 oz): sold in pairs. Maple, Slate and Cream only.
- **Soup Bowl** (20 oz): wide and shallow. All six glazes.
- **Teapot** (32 oz): comes with a stainless steel infuser. Maple and Slate only.
- **Seconds**: pieces with small cosmetic marks, 30% off. Seconds are final sale.

Every piece is handmade, so sizes and colors vary a little from the photos. Small differences in glaze, tiny pinholes and slightly different heights are normal and are not defects.

## Ordering and payment

- We accept credit and debit cards, PayPal and Maple Mugs gift cards.
- Orders can be changed or canceled within 2 hours of being placed. After that, the order may already be packed.
- To change an order, the customer replies to their order confirmation email.
- We don't offer payment plans or cash on delivery.
- Prices are in US dollars and include all fees except shipping and local taxes.

## Shipping

- We ship from Vermont, Monday to Friday. Orders placed before noon Eastern time ship the same day.
- **Standard shipping** (US): 3 to 6 business days, $6. Free on orders over $60.
- **Express shipping** (US): 1 to 2 business days, $18.
- **International shipping**: Canada, the UK and the EU only. 7 to 14 business days, $25. Customs fees are paid by the customer.
- Every order gets a tracking link by email when it ships.
- If tracking shows no movement for 7 business days, we open an investigation with the carrier and send a replacement or a refund, whichever the customer prefers.
- If a package shows as delivered but the customer can't find it, ask them to check with neighbors and their building's mail room, and to wait one more day. If it's still missing, we open a claim with the carrier.

## Address changes

- Before the order ships: reply to the confirmation email with the new address. We update it for free.
- After the order ships: we can't change the address, but the customer can request a redirect through the carrier's tracking page. Redirect fees are paid by the customer.

## Returns and refunds

- Customers can return unused items within 30 days of delivery for a full refund to the original payment method.
- Return shipping is free with the prepaid label from our returns page: maplemugs.example/returns.
- Refunds are sent within 5 business days after the return arrives at the studio.
- Used items, personalized items and Seconds cannot be returned.
- After 30 days, we can't accept returns, but we can offer store credit for unused items up to 60 days after delivery.
- Gift returns: the person who received the gift can get store credit without telling the buyer.

## Damaged or broken items

- If something arrives broken, the customer sends one photo of the item and one of the box within 7 days of delivery.
- We send a free replacement right away. The customer doesn't need to send the broken piece back.
- If the glaze or color is out of stock, the customer can choose another glaze or a full refund.

## Care

- All mugs, bowls and teapots are dishwasher safe and microwave safe.
- They are not oven safe and not safe on a stove.
- Avoid sudden temperature changes, like pouring boiling water into a mug that just came out of the fridge.
- Teapot infusers can go in the dishwasher. Hand washing keeps them shiny longer.
- Small marks from metal spoons can be removed with a little baking soda and a soft cloth.

## Personalization

- Classic Mugs and Big Morning Mugs can be personalized with up to 12 letters or numbers, stamped into the clay before firing.
- Personalization adds $8 per piece and 7 business days to the shipping time.
- Personalized items cannot be returned unless they arrive broken or the stamp has a mistake that we made.

## Gift cards

- Digital gift cards from $25 to $200, sent by email on the date the buyer chooses.
- Gift cards never expire and can be used on several orders.
- Gift cards can't be exchanged for cash.

## Wholesale and cafes

- Cafes and shops can order 24 or more pieces at wholesale prices.
- Wholesale orders take 4 to 6 weeks because every piece is made to order.
- For wholesale questions, the customer writes to wholesale@maplemugs.example. Don't quote wholesale prices in chat.

## Contact and hours

- Email: help@maplemugs.example. The team answers within one business day.
- The studio is open to visitors on Saturdays from 10 am to 4 pm. No orders are packed on Saturdays.
- We don't have a phone line.

## Things you must never do

- Never share another customer's name, address or order details.
- Never ask for card numbers or passwords.
- Never invent a discount code. The only current code is WELCOME10 (10% off a first order).
- Never guess. If you're not sure, say so and point the customer to help@maplemugs.example.

lines.say: And here's the bot without caching. The handbook goes into the system prompt, and the customer's question into the message.

do.text:
"""Answers a question. The handbook is sent every time."""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
HANDBOOK = Path("handbook.md").read_text(encoding="utf-8")

reply = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    max_tokens=300,
    system="Answer Maple Mugs customers.\n\n" + HANDBOOK,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": sys.argv[1]}],
)
print(reply.content[0].text)
print(f"input tokens: {reply.usage.input_tokens}")

lines.say: Let's ask two questions, and look at the input tokens.

do.text: python no_cache.py "Are your mugs dishwasher safe?"
out: Yes! All our mugs are dishwasher and microwave safe. They're not oven safe, though.
Standard US shipping is free on orders over $60. Otherwise it's $6.

lines.say: Almost 1,500 input tokens, each time. The question is only a few words. The rest is the same handbook, processed and billed again and again.
lines.tts: Almost fifteen hundred input tokens, each time. The question is only a few words. The rest is the same handbook, processed and billed again and again.

lines.say: Step one: put the stable part first.
Same start as before. But this time, the system prompt is a list of two text blocks: the short instruction, then the whole handbook.

do.text:
"""Answers a customer question. The handbook is cached."""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
HANDBOOK = Path("handbook.md").read_text(encoding="utf-8")

# 1. Stable part first: the same in every request
system = [
    {"type": "text", "text": "Answer Maple Mugs customers."},
    {"type": "text", "text": HANDBOOK,
     "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}},  # cache up to here
]

lines.say: Why this order? The cache only matches the start of a prompt. So everything that's the same in every request goes first.
Step two: mark the cache breakpoint.
On the handbook block, I add cache control, type ephemeral. That's the breakpoint. Everything up to here, and including this block, is the prefix that gets cached.
Then the request. The customer's question changes every time, so it goes after the breakpoint, in the messages.

do.text:
# 2. The part that changes goes after the breakpoint
reply = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    max_tokens=300,
    system=system,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": sys.argv[1]}],
)
print(reply.content[0].text)

lines.say: That's the key rule: put the breakpoint on the last block that stays the same. Never on the part that changes.
Step three: check the usage.
Every response tells you what happened with the cache. I print three numbers: tokens written to the cache, tokens read from it, and new tokens after the breakpoint.

do.text:
# 3. Check the cache
u = reply.usage
print(f"written: {u.cache_creation_input_tokens}  "
      f"read: {u.cache_read_input_tokens}  new: {u.input_tokens}")

lines.say: Let's ask the first question.

do.text: python ask.py "Are your mugs dishwasher safe?"
out: Yes! All our mugs are dishwasher and microwave safe. They're not oven safe, though.

lines.say: The first request wrote about 1,500 tokens to the cache. Only twelve tokens were new: the question.
lines.tts: The first request wrote about fifteen hundred tokens to the cache. Only twelve tokens were new: the question.

lines.say: Now a second question, within five minutes.

out: Standard US shipping is free on orders over $60. Otherwise it's $6.

lines.say: This time, the whole handbook was read from the cache. Nothing written. That's a cache hit.
If both numbers are zero, nothing was cached. Usually the prompt is too short, or something changed in the prefix.
Step four: count the savings.
This little script does the math for a thousand questions a day, using Claude Sonnet 5.5 prices, for the handbook part of the prompt.
lines.tts: This little script does the math for a thousand questions a day, using Claude Sonnet five point five prices, for the handbook part of the prompt.

do.text:
"""Cost of 1,000 questions a day (the handbook part only)."""
# Claude Sonnet 5.5, dollars per million tokens (October 2026)
BASE, WRITE, READ = 2.00, 2.50, 0.10

HANDBOOK = 1_500    # tokens in the cached part
QUESTIONS = 1_000   # a day, all within the cache lifetime


def dollars(tokens, price):
    return tokens * price / 1_000_000


no_cache = QUESTIONS * dollars(HANDBOOK, BASE)
cached = (dollars(HANDBOOK, WRITE)
          + (QUESTIONS - 1) * dollars(HANDBOOK, READ))

print(f"No cache: ${no_cache:.2f}")
print(f"Cached:   ${cached:.2f}")
print(f"Saved:    {1 - cached / no_cache:.0%}")

lines.say: Without caching, every question pays the base price. With caching, one write, then 999 cheap reads.
lines.tts: Without caching, every question pays the base price. With caching, one write, then nine hundred and ninety-nine cheap reads.

lines.say: Let's run it, and compare the two numbers.
Three dollars become fifteen cents. Ninety-five percent saved on that part, and the bigger the handbook, the more you save.
The files also include an offline test, so you can try everything with no API key.

cards.title: Stable first, changes last
cards.text: Dates and per-request data at the **end**

cards.title: Parallel requests? Wait
cards.text: Send one first: the cache starts with its response

lines.say: Four tips.
One: stable content first, changing content last. A date or a timestamp at the top of your prompt breaks the cache on every request.
Two: always check the usage. If both cache numbers are zero, nothing was cached, and you get no error.
Three: for parallel requests, send one first. The cache is only there once the first response starts.
And four: if requests come more than five minutes apart, you can use a one-hour cache. Writing it costs twice the normal input price.

scenes.heading: Recap
items: Caching stores the **prefix**: the start of your prompt
Stable part first, then **cache_control** on its last block
One write, then [[cheap reads]]: check the usage

lines.say: Let's recap.
Prompt caching stores the prefix, the start of your prompt, for five minutes.
Put the stable part first, and mark its last block with cache control.
You pay for one write, then cheap reads. And the usage numbers tell you if it worked.
